title: AI speeds things up. But how far?
description: AI lowered the cost of experimenting, but output isn't a decision. How the process changes and why evaluating matters more the faster we create.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: an explorable design system, with tokens, components, contrast and governance.

data.a: The speed at which we can build digital products has changed.
data.b: An idea that used to take days to become a prototype can now show up in minutes.
data.c: All of this can speed up a product team's work a lot.
data.d: But there's a question I think matters:
data.e: Because being faster at doing the wrong thing is still a problem.

blocks.text: AI lowered the cost of experimenting
This is one of the parts I find most interesting.
Before, creating a new solution had a fairly high cost.
Now we can explore many more possibilities before deciding.
That's a huge opportunity for designers.
We can use AI to generate alternatives and test hypotheses quickly.
But it also creates a new problem.
If it's now easy to create 20 solutions, who decides which two deserve to be tested?
Output isn't a decision

items: This may be the main point

blocks.caption: The faster we create, the more evaluating matters.

blocks.text: Imagine a tool generates five versions of a screen.
They all look good.
Which one do you pick?
If the answer is:
“The prettiest one.”
We have a problem.
The decision should take into account:

items: what problem we're trying to solve;
what hypothesis we want to test.

blocks.text: That's judgment.
Speed can hide problems
When a process gets very fast, there's a tendency to skip steps.
But maybe nobody asked:
Where did this solution come from?
What problem does it solve?
What evidence do we have?
What could go wrong?
Who does it not work for?
That's one of the risks of speed.
It's not that AI necessarily produces bad solutions.
It's that it makes it easier to accept a solution before understanding it.
The designer's critical eye
I believe one of the most important skills for a designer in the age of AI is exactly this:
knowing how to look at a solution and question it.
It's not enough to recognize whether an interface looks nice.
We need to notice:
Is important information hidden?
Does the hierarchy make sense?
Is the language clear?
Does the flow demand unnecessary effort?
Does the solution work for different users?
Is there an error state?
Is there an empty state?
What happens when the user changes their mind?
Are there any accessibility issues?
Does the solution actually solve the problem?
This critical eye isn't a detail.
It's a core part of design work.
AI doesn't automatically know your user
An AI knows a lot of patterns.
But your product isn't “the average” of every product out there.
If that information doesn't make it into the process, AI tends to produce something generic.
That's why context is becoming an increasingly important part of UX work.
Maybe the new job is giving context
If AI can generate an interface, someone has to say:
For whom?
For what problem?
In what situation?
With what rules?
With which components?
In what language?
With what data?
With what constraints?
With what goals?
That information shapes the result.
It's like asking someone to build a house.
If all you say is:
“Build a house.”
They'll have to imagine the rest.
But if you explain who will live in it, how the house will be used, what the lot is like, what the needs are and what constraints exist, the result changes.
Something similar happens with AI.
The faster we create, the more evaluating matters
It's an interesting paradox.
AI increases the speed of production.
But that can increase the number of things that need to be evaluated.
The production step got faster.
Our capacity to evaluate has to keep up.
That's why research, usability testing, metrics and critique still matter.
The question changes

items.q: “How long do we need to build this?”
“How long do we need to evaluate this?”
“How do we know this deserves to be built?”

data.b: Because the bottleneck may stop being production.

blocks.text: AI can raise the quality of the work
I don't see AI only as a tool to go faster.
It can also let designers do things they wouldn't have had time to do before.
But only if the time saved is used to think better.
If we use the time saved just to produce even more, we may not be taking advantage of the full potential.
The new process can look different
I like to think of it like this:

blocks.caption: AI speeds up production, but it doesn't replace understanding and evaluating.

blocks.text: Problem → Context → AI → Exploration → Critique → Testing → Decision

items: And it shouldn't end it either

blocks.text: In between there's a big opportunity for designers.
In the end, speed is only one part
Being fast matters.
But it isn't enough.
A product doesn't gain value because it was produced quickly.
It gains value because it solves a relevant problem in a way that works for people and for the business.

items: AI can speed up our process

blocks.text: But we still need to know where to put that capacity.
Maybe a designer's edge in the coming years won't be creating faster.
Maybe it'll be deciding better what's worth creating.
